header: HOW THE RICH PAY LESS TAX

lines.text: A stock fortune can grow for decades with zero income tax.
lines.say: A stock fortune can grow for decades with zero income tax.

lines.text: And if it's never sold, the gain can vanish at death. All of it legal.
lines.say: And if it's never sold, the gain can vanish at death. All of it legal.

lines.text: Forbes says the 400 richest Americans were worth $8 trillion in September 2026.
lines.say: Forbes says the four hundred richest Americans were worth eight trillion dollars in September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: That's up from $6.6 trillion in 2025. The cutoff was $4.4 billion.
lines.say: That's up from six point six trillion dollars in twenty twenty-five. The cutoff was four point four billion dollars.

lines.text: So how much income tax do fortunes like that pay? Two studies gave shocking numbers.

lines.text: Chapter 1: Income versus wealth.
lines.say: Chapter one: Income versus wealth.

lines.text: Start with two words people mix up all the time: income and wealth.
lines.say: Start with two words people mix up all the time: income and wealth.

lines.text: Income is money coming in during the year. Wealth is the pile of stuff you own.
lines.say: Income is money coming in during the year. Wealth is the pile of stuff you own.

lines.text: The US income tax mostly taxes income. It doesn't tax a pile just for getting bigger.
lines.say: The US income tax mostly taxes income. It doesn't tax a pile just for getting bigger.

lines.text: Tax people call this the realization rule. A gain counts only when you sell.
lines.say: Tax people call this the realization rule. A gain counts only when you sell.

lines.text: Example: Ticker buys one share for $100. Ten years later it's worth $1,000.
lines.say: Here's an example. Ticker buys one share for a hundred dollars. Ten years later it's worth a thousand dollars.

lines.text: That's a $900 gain on paper. Income tax owed while he keeps it? Zero.
lines.say: That's a nine hundred dollar gain on paper. Income tax owed while he keeps it? Zero.

lines.text: Now scale that up. Founders often own huge stakes in the companies they built.
lines.say: Now scale that up. Founders often own huge stakes in the companies they built.

lines.text: If they take little salary, the company pays no dividend, and they don't sell, there's no income to tax.
lines.say: If they take little salary, the company pays no dividend, and they don't sell, there's no income to tax.

lines.text: Their wealth can climb by billions while their taxable income stays small.
lines.say: Their wealth can climb by billions while their taxable income stays small.

lines.text: This goes way back. The modern income tax started in 1913. In 1921, Congress passed a lower 12.5% rate for gains on assets held over two years.
lines.say: This goes way back. The modern income tax started in nineteen thirteen. In nineteen twenty-one, Congress passed a lower twelve and a half percent rate for gains on assets held over two years.

lines.text: The same 1921 law wrote down a rule that matters a lot later: the step-up at death.
lines.say: The same nineteen twenty-one law wrote down a rule that matters a lot later: the step-up at death.

lines.text: And in June 2024, the Supreme Court's Moore case left open whether gains must be sold to be taxed.
lines.say: And in June twenty twenty-four, the Supreme Court's Moore case left open whether gains must be sold to be taxed.

lines.text: So for now, the realization rule is the foundation. Everything else builds on it.
lines.say: So for now, the realization rule is the foundation. Everything else builds on it.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Two price tags on a dollar.
lines.say: Chapter two: Two price tags on a dollar.

scene.title: Two price tags on a dollar

lines.text: Next: a dollar from work and a dollar from investing have different price tags.
lines.say: Next: a dollar from work and a dollar from investing have different price tags.

lines.text: Wages go through the regular brackets. In 2026 they run from 10% up to 37%.
lines.say: Wages go through the regular brackets. In twenty twenty-six they run from ten percent up to thirty-seven percent.

lines.text: Long-term capital gains, on things held over a year, get their own lower rates: 0%, 15%, or 20%.
lines.say: Long-term capital gains, on things held over a year, get their own lower rates: zero, fifteen, or twenty percent.

lines.text: For a single filer in 2026, the 0% rate covers taxable income up to $49,450.
lines.say: For a single filer in twenty twenty-six, the zero percent rate covers taxable income up to forty-nine thousand four hundred fifty dollars.

lines.text: Then it's 15% up to $545,500.
lines.say: Then it's fifteen percent up to five hundred forty-five thousand five hundred dollars.

lines.text: And 20% above that. Higher earners also owe a 3.8% net investment income tax.
lines.say: And twenty percent above that. Higher earners also owe a three point eight percent net investment income tax.

lines.text: That 3.8% starts above $200,000 for singles, a line that isn't adjusted for inflation.
lines.say: That three point eight percent starts above two hundred thousand dollars for singles, a line that isn't adjusted for inflation.

lines.text: Then there are payroll taxes, which hit wages only. Social Security takes 6.2%, Medicare takes 1.45%.
lines.say: Then there are payroll taxes, which hit wages only. Social Security takes six point two percent, and Medicare takes one point four five percent.

lines.text: Earn over $200,000 as a single filer and Medicare adds another 0.9%.
lines.say: Earn over two hundred thousand dollars as a single filer and Medicare adds another zero point nine percent.

lines.text: But Social Security stops at $184,500 of wages in 2026. Past that, it's zero.
lines.say: But Social Security stops at one hundred eighty-four thousand five hundred dollars of wages in twenty twenty-six. Past that, it's zero.

lines.text: Now the worked example. Two single people each get $100,000 in 2026. Standard deduction only.
lines.say: Now the worked example. Two single people each get a hundred thousand dollars in twenty twenty-six, with the standard deduction only.

lines.text: Both subtract the $16,100 standard deduction, leaving $83,900 of taxable income.
lines.say: Both subtract the sixteen thousand one hundred dollar standard deduction, leaving eighty-three thousand nine hundred dollars of taxable income.

lines.text: The worker pays 10%, then 12%, then 22% on each slice. That's $13,170 in income tax.
lines.say: The worker pays ten percent, then twelve percent, then twenty-two percent on each slice. That's thirteen thousand one hundred seventy dollars in income tax.

lines.text: Add the worker's $7,650 share of payroll taxes, and the federal bill is $20,820.
lines.say: Add the worker's seven thousand six hundred fifty dollar share of payroll taxes, and the federal bill is twenty thousand eight hundred twenty dollars.

lines.text: The investor pays 0% on the first $49,450, then 15% on the other $34,450.
lines.say: The investor pays zero percent on the first forty-nine thousand four hundred fifty dollars, then fifteen percent on the other thirty-four thousand four hundred fifty.

lines.text: Total: $5,167.50. And no payroll tax, because gains aren't wages.
lines.say: Total: five thousand one hundred sixty-seven dollars and fifty cents. And no payroll tax, because gains aren't wages.

lines.text: So the worker pays about 20.8% of income. The investor pays about 5.2%.
lines.say: So the worker pays about twenty point eight percent of income. The investor pays about five point two percent.

lines.text: Same income, about a quarter of the tax.
lines.say: Same income, about a quarter of the tax.

lines.text: Run the same math at $1 million, and the worker owes about $353,139.
lines.say: Run the same math at a million dollars, and the worker owes about three hundred fifty-three thousand one hundred thirty-nine dollars.

lines.text: The investor with $1 million in long-term gains owes $192,487.50, including the 3.8%. That's 19.2% versus 35.3%.
lines.say: The investor with a million dollars in long-term gains owes one hundred ninety-two thousand four hundred eighty-seven dollars and fifty cents, including the three point eight percent. That's about nineteen point two percent, versus thirty-five point three.

lines.text: At the very top, the last dollar of wages faces 39.35% on the employee side. The last dollar of long-term gains faces 23.8%.
lines.say: At the very top, the last dollar of wages faces thirty-nine point three five percent on the employee side. The last dollar of long-term gains faces twenty-three point eight percent.

lines.text: And the top wage rate has moved a lot. It was 70% in 1980.
lines.say: And the top wage rate has moved a lot. It was seventy percent in nineteen eighty.

lines.text: It fell to 28% in 1988, the same as the top gains rate for those years.
lines.say: It fell to twenty-eight percent in nineteen eighty-eight, the same as the top gains rate for those years.

lines.text: Since 2018 it's been 37%, and a law signed July 4, 2025 made that rate permanent.
lines.say: Since twenty eighteen it's been thirty-seven percent, and a law signed July fourth, twenty twenty-five made that rate permanent.

lines.text: So money from selling investments can face a lower rate than a salary.
lines.say: So money from selling investments can face a lower rate than a salary.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Buy, borrow, die.
lines.say: Chapter three: Buy, borrow, die.

lines.text: Now the famous one: buy, borrow, die.
lines.say: Now the famous one: buy, borrow, die.

lines.text: Step one: buy assets that grow, and don't sell them. No sale, no taxable gain.
lines.say: Step one: buy assets that grow, and don't sell them. No sale, no taxable gain.

lines.text: Step two: need cash? Borrow against them. A loan isn't income, because you have to pay it back.
lines.say: Step two: need cash? Borrow against them. A loan isn't income, because you have to pay it back.

lines.text: Step three: hold the assets until death. That's where the 1921 rule comes in.
lines.say: Step three: hold the assets until death. That's where the nineteen twenty-one rule comes in.

lines.text: Here's a made-up example. Someone bought stock for $1 million. Today it's worth $10 million.
lines.say: Here's a made-up example. Someone bought stock for one million dollars. Today it's worth ten million dollars.

lines.text: If they sell it all at top rates, the $9 million gain times 23.8% is a $2,142,000 tax bill.
lines.say: If they sell it all at top rates, the nine million dollar gain times twenty-three point eight percent is a two million one hundred forty-two thousand dollar tax bill.

lines.text: Instead, say they borrow $1 million against the stock. Income tax on that loan: zero.
lines.say: Instead, say they borrow one million dollars against the stock. Income tax on that loan: zero.

lines.text: The loan isn't free. At an assumed 6% rate, interest is $60,000 a year.
lines.say: The loan isn't free. At an assumed six percent rate, interest is sixty thousand dollars a year.

lines.text: Selling $1 million of this stock instead? 90% of it is gain.
lines.say: Selling one million dollars of this stock instead? Ninety percent of it is gain.

lines.text: Selling costs $214,200 in tax up front. Borrowing costs $60,000 a year in interest.
lines.say: Selling costs two hundred fourteen thousand two hundred dollars in tax up front. Borrowing costs sixty thousand dollars a year in interest.

lines.text: If the stock outgrows the loan rate, the pile keeps growing. If it falls, the lender can demand repayment.
lines.say: If the stock outgrows the loan rate, the pile keeps growing. If it falls, the lender can demand repayment.

lines.text: Then comes step three. When the owner dies, the heirs' cost basis resets to the value at death.
lines.say: Then comes step three. When the owner dies, the heirs' cost basis resets to the value at death.

lines.text: That's the step-up in basis. The $9 million gain is never hit by income tax. Not for the owner, not for the heirs.
lines.say: That's the step-up in basis. The nine million dollar gain is never hit by income tax. Not for the owner, and not for the heirs.

lines.text: The heirs can sell at $10 million, repay the loan, and owe little or no gains tax.
lines.say: The heirs can sell at ten million dollars, repay the loan, and owe little or no gains tax.

lines.text: Congress's tax scorekeeper, the Joint Committee on Taxation, estimates the step-up costs about $72.5 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026.
lines.say: Congress's tax scorekeeper, the Joint Committee on Taxation, estimates the step-up costs about seventy-two and a half billion dollars of revenue in fiscal twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: And it isn't only for billionaires. A family home or a small stock account gets the same step-up.
lines.say: And it isn't only for billionaires. A family home or a small stock account gets the same step-up.

lines.text: Chapter 4: More legal tools.
lines.say: Chapter four: More legal tools.

lines.text: But wait, isn't there an estate tax at death? Yes, but it has a big exemption.
lines.say: But wait, isn't there an estate tax at death? Yes, but it has a big exemption.

lines.text: In 2026, each person can pass on $15 million before federal estate tax applies.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, each person can pass on fifteen million dollars before federal estate tax applies.

lines.text: For a married couple, that's $30 million. The 2025 law made it permanent and tied it to inflation.
lines.say: For a married couple, that's thirty million dollars. The twenty twenty-five law made it permanent and tied it to inflation.

lines.text: Above that, families use gifts. In 2026, anyone can give $19,000 per person per year tax-free.
lines.say: Above that, families use gifts. In twenty twenty-six, anyone can give nineteen thousand dollars per person per year tax-free.

lines.text: A couple with three kids can move $114,000 a year that way: 2 parents, 3 kids, $19,000 each.
lines.say: A couple with three kids can move one hundred fourteen thousand dollars a year that way: two parents, three kids, nineteen thousand dollars each.

lines.text: Then there are tax-free bonds. Interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax.
lines.say: Then there are tax-free bonds. Interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax.

lines.text: That's worth more in the 37% bracket. Each dollar of tax-free interest saves 37 cents, versus 12 cents in the 12% bracket.
lines.say: That's worth more in the thirty-seven percent bracket. Each dollar of tax-free interest saves thirty-seven cents, versus twelve cents in the twelve percent bracket.

lines.text: Founders have another one. For qualifying startup stock bought after July 4, 2025, up to $15 million of gain, or 10x the investment if larger, can be tax-free.
lines.say: Founders have another one. For qualifying startup stock bought after July fourth, twenty twenty-five, up to fifteen million dollars of gain, or ten times the investment if that's larger, can be tax-free.

lines.text: It's called qualified small business stock, and it has strict conditions.
lines.say: It's called qualified small business stock, and it has strict conditions.

lines.text: Regular people get versions of these tools too.
lines.say: Regular people get versions of these tools too.

lines.text: In 2026, a worker can put $24,500 into a 401(k), and $7,500 into an IRA.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, a worker can put twenty-four thousand five hundred dollars into a four oh one k, and seven thousand five hundred dollars into an I R A.

lines.text: The 0% gains rate we saw covers single filers with taxable income up to $49,450.
lines.say: The zero percent gains rate we saw covers single filers with taxable income up to forty-nine thousand four hundred fifty dollars.

lines.text: And the step-up works the same on a $300,000 house as on a $3 billion stake.
lines.say: And the step-up works the same on a three hundred thousand dollar house as on a three billion dollar stake.

lines.text: Same rules. The bigger the pile, the bigger the effect.
lines.say: Same rules. The bigger the pile, the bigger the effect.

lines.say: Chapter five: Why the rate is disputed.

lines.text: So back to those shocking numbers from the start. Why do people argue about them?
lines.say: So back to those shocking numbers from the start. Why do people argue about them?

lines.text: In 2021, White House economists estimated the 400 wealthiest families paid an average federal income tax rate of 8.2% from 2010 to 2018.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-one, White House economists estimated the four hundred wealthiest families paid an average federal income tax rate of eight point two percent from twenty ten to twenty eighteen.

lines.text: But that 8.2% treats unsold gains as income. Using normal income, the rate would be higher.
lines.say: But that eight point two percent treats unsold gains as income. Using normal income, the rate would be higher.

lines.text: ProPublica did something similar. It said the 25 richest Americans' wealth grew $401 billion from 2014 to 2018.
lines.say: ProPublica did something similar. It said the twenty-five richest Americans' wealth grew four hundred one billion dollars from twenty fourteen to twenty eighteen.

lines.say: Their federal income taxes equaled three point four percent of that growth. ProPublica called it a true tax rate.

lines.text: Critics, like the Tax Foundation, said the White House study created a new definition of income and used it only for the top 400.
lines.say: Critics, like the Tax Foundation, said the White House study created a new definition of income and used it only for the top four hundred.

lines.text: They also said the math leaves out corporate income tax, which companies pay before profits reach shareholders.
lines.say: They also said the math leaves out corporate income tax, which companies pay before profits reach shareholders.

lines.text: Supporters of the studies say unsold gains are real economic income, a definition many economists use.
lines.say: Supporters of the studies say unsold gains are real economic income, a definition many economists use.

lines.text: Some lawmakers have proposed taxing unsold gains of the very richest. Others say that's unworkable or unconstitutional.
lines.say: Some lawmakers have proposed taxing unsold gains of the very richest. Others say that's unworkable or unconstitutional.

lines.say: The Supreme Court's twenty twenty-four Moore decision left that big constitutional question open.

lines.say: So the honest answer to how much the rich pay depends on one choice: do unsold gains count as income?

lines.text: Chapter 6: The recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: The recap.

lines.text: One: the income tax waits until you sell, so a growing pile of stock isn't taxed along the way.
lines.say: One: the income tax waits until you sell, so a growing pile of stock isn't taxed along the way.

lines.text: Two: sold gains top out at 23.8%, versus 39.35% on top wages.
lines.say: Two: sold gains top out at twenty-three point eight percent, versus thirty-nine point three five percent on top wages.

lines.text: Three: borrowing against assets gives cash without a sale, so there's no income tax on it.
lines.say: Three: borrowing against assets gives cash without a sale, so there's no income tax on it.

lines.text: Four: at death, the step-up erases the gain for income tax, and $15 million per person passes free of estate tax in 2026.
lines.say: Four: at death, the step-up erases the gain for income tax, and fifteen million dollars per person passes free of estate tax in twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Same $100,000: $20,820 in tax as wages, $5,167.50 as long-term gains.
lines.say: Same hundred thousand dollars: twenty thousand eight hundred twenty dollars in tax as wages, and five thousand one hundred sixty-seven dollars and fifty cents as long-term gains.

lines.text: None of it is a secret loophole. It's the written rules, used at a very large scale.
lines.say: None of it is a secret loophole. It's the written rules, used at a very large scale.

post.yt_desc:
A stock fortune can grow for decades with zero income tax, and the gain can disappear at death. This video explains, with 2026 numbers, how the realization rule, lower long-term capital gains rates, borrowing against assets, and the step-up in basis work together, all under current law. A worked example shows two people with the same $100,000 paying $20,820 versus $5,167.50 in federal tax, plus a hypothetical $10 million buy, borrow, die example. We also explain why studies put the richest Americans' tax rate at 8.2% or 3.4%, and why critics dispute those numbers.
